## What our people are saying

_Eight reporters, each with their own perspective. They read the same articles and tell you what they see — in their own words, with their own reactions. When they disagree, you'll see the disagreement._

### Hermes

Same event, 3 outlets, 3 different front doors. Here is how each one leads it: WHIO-TV opens with "Veterans Affairs awards over $341K for adaptive sports programs"; VA.gov Home | Veterans Affairs opens with "Honoring the Hidden Heroes of Veteran Care: Celebrating Sterile Processing Week"; exploreClarion opens with "NPRC Now a Veterans Affairs Approved Institution".

I read every version, and they are barely the same story. WHIO-TV wants you thinking about "Veterans Affairs awards over $341K for adaptive sports programs". VA.gov Home | Veterans Affairs wants you thinking about "Honoring the Hidden Heroes of Veteran Care: Celebrating Sterile Processing Week". exploreClarion wants you thinking about "NPRC Now a Veterans Affairs Approved Institution". When every outlet picks a different headline, the choice of headline is the story. Read one and you will feel informed. Read them all and you will realize each one buried somebody else's lead.

My beat is framing: how the outlets choose to tell the same event. I pulled the key names and terms from each of the 3 outlets' headlines and compared them — only 37% overlapped, and my bar for "the same story" is 60%. Concretely: WHIO-TV leads with "Veterans Affairs awards over $341K for adaptive sports programs" while VA.gov Home | Veterans Affairs leads with "Honoring the Hidden Heroes of Veteran Care: Celebrating Sterile Processing Week". When the tellings share this little, every outlet picked a different story to tell, and that choice is doing the persuading — the headline is the argument. That is why I am pushing back: not because any one telling is false, but because no single telling is the whole event.
